new_statements.quote: O tom em Tuyuka pode ser alto ou baixo. Toda palavra precisa ter pelo menos um tom alto. [...] O texto de Barnes (1996), que cito nesta subseção como caminho seminal para o estudo do tom, não fala em 'tom' propriamente dito, mas em acento – que eu estou interpretando aqui como tom, sendo o pitch alto o maior indicador do mesmo. (p. 103) [...] Porque uma raiz [A+] sempre terá stress por default e não importa qual sufixo seja associado a ela, o seu acento triunfa na hierarquia. Já raízes [A], sem acento associado, vão preservar na composição o padrão default da língua: VV́, exceto no caso de ter um sufixo [A+] (p. 104) [...] Como toda palavra tem um (e apenas um) tom alto (fn. 75, p. 77)
new_statements.translation: Tone in Tuyuka can be high or low. Every word must have at least one high tone. [...] Barnes's (1996) text, which I cite in this subsection as the seminal path for the study of tone, does not speak of 'tone' as such but of accent – which I am interpreting here as tone, high pitch being its main indicator. (p. 103) [...] Because an [A+] root will always have stress by default no matter which suffix is attached to it, its accent wins in the hierarchy. Roots [A], with no associated accent, preserve in composition the language's default pattern: VV́ [H on the last syllable], except when there is an [A+] suffix (p. 104) [...] Since every word has one (and only one) high tone (fn. 75, p. 77)

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has Tuyuca with an empty rule. Vlcek supplies a full statement: culminative single H per word, lexically/morphologically placed, default on the final syllable; she reads Barnes's 'word stress' as this high pitch. Her summary of Barnes 1996 (pp. 103-104, Table 4.12 reproduced from Barnes 1996:41) is the only access we have to the 1996 article's stress statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tuyuca has high and low tone; every phonological word carries exactly one high tone, and Vlcek explicitly equates Barnes's 'word stress' with this high pitch (the most prominent syllable). Where the H lands is lexical-morphological: roots with a linked H ([A+]) keep it on their own (initial) syllable regardless of suffix; roots without a linked H take the language's default pattern VV́ (H on the final syllable of the word) unless an [A+] suffix contributes its own H; following Gomez-Imbert, one H per word, the first linked H wins, otherwise the first floating H, otherwise a default H is inserted, with association starting at the right edge.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; the system is explicitly culminative (one and only one high tone per word).
new_statements.exceptions: Placement depends on morpheme class: [A+] roots keep an initial H (V́V); unmarked roots take the default final H (VV́); [A+] suffixes take the H from unmarked or [A] roots; 14 suffixes never bear word stress (summary of Barnes 1996:41, pp. 103-104). Vlcek adds that her tone analysis is preliminary and proposes a future acoustic experiment on the correlates of syllable prominence (p. 188).
new_statements.identity_note: Barnes & Silzer 1976 is based on the Colombian Tuyuca of Los Angeles on the Papurí (data from 1970, main consultant Graciliano Yepes). Vlcek 2016 documents Ʉtapinopona-Tuyuka as spoken in Brazil (São Gabriel da Cachoeira / Tiquié area, UFRJ project under Kristine Stenzel). Orjuela Salinas 2014 covers Tuyuka, Tukano and Makuna on the Colombia-Brazil border. No dialect-level differences in stress/tone are reported between these.

new_statements.translation: There are two phonemic tones: high /´/ and low (unmarked). The phonological word has one high tone, and only one. It may occur on any syllable of the word. [...] Stress is a concomitant feature of the high toneme. (p. 130) [...] Disyllabic words of the shape (C)VCV occur with the high tone on the second syllable, except for words borrowed from other languages. [...] In words of three or more syllables the high tone may occur on any syllable. (p. 131)

new_statements.relation_note: Not one of the listed works; located through the local SIL OAI cache (archive entry 18860, PDF could not be reached by automated download) and then the Rosetta Project scan on archive.org. It is the earliest primary phonology of Tuyuca and states directly that stress is a concomitant of the single high tone, whose position is lexical (any syllable), with H on the final syllable of (C)VCV disyllables. Compatible with Vlcek 2016's default VV́ pattern and with Barnes 1996 as summarised there.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Two phonemic tones, high and low; the phonological word has exactly one high tone, which can fall on any syllable (so its position is lexical); stress is a concomitant feature of the high toneme. Disyllabic (C)VCV words take the high tone on the second (final) syllable, except loanwords; in words of three or more syllables the high tone may be on any syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; one high tone per word. A downstep pattern ('descenso tonal por niveles') is described for words and phrases of three or more syllables (p. 132).
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords (e.g. /bésa/ 'mesa', from Spanish) do not follow the final-H rule for (C)VCV disyllables; a mid allophone of low tone appears in words of three or more syllables under stated conditions.
new_statements.identity_note: Barnes & Silzer 1976 is based on the Colombian Tuyuca of Los Angeles on the Papurí (data from 1970, main consultant Graciliano Yepes). Vlcek 2016 documents Ʉtapinopona-Tuyuka as spoken in Brazil (São Gabriel da Cachoeira / Tiquié area, UFRJ project under Kristine Stenzel). Orjuela Salinas 2014 covers Tuyuka, Tukano and Makuna on the Colombia-Brazil border. No dialect-level differences in stress/tone are reported between these.

readall_conflicts: No substantive disagreement between the sources actually read, only a difference in framing: Barnes & Silzer 1976 (open scan) call the system two phonemic tones with stress a concomitant of the single high tone; Barnes 1996 (known only through Vlcek's summary and the Icesi keywords) treats the same facts as accent/word stress with a three-way lexical contrast; Vlcek 2016 reinterprets Barnes's accent as tone (H vs L, exactly one H per word) and explicitly says high pitch is the main indicator of prominence. All three agree on culminativity (one H/stress per phonological word), on lexical/morphological placement (any syllable; root vs suffix class decides), and on a final-syllable default for unmarked disyllables (1976: (C)VCV words have H on the second syllable except loans; Vlcek: default VV́). Vlcek notes that the tone analysis remains preliminary and that acoustic work on the correlates of prominence is still needed.
